requirement:
A successful `ValidationContext::read` records the node's identity and the
fingerprint of the returned contents, under
{cite}`requirements.sdk.graph.evidence.node_inputs`. A failed read records no
successful observation. The evidence becomes stale when a later read of that
node has a different fingerprint; a failure to resolve it is reported by
{cite}`requirements.sdk.graph.evidence.checking_records`.

For a Rust caller, the SDK records the fingerprint when `read` returns the
contents. For an agent, the harness puts a tool result in the next request to
the model and records the fingerprint once the provider responds successfully.
That successful exchange is *delivery*. For example, suppose the tool reads a
function that returns `3`, and someone changes it to return `4` before the
provider responds. The model saw the version that returns `3`, so the SDK
records the fingerprint it computed from that version. Reading the function
again at this point would record a fingerprint for code the model never saw.

structural: I found no structural obligation in `requirements.sdk.graph.validation-context.read_node.inputs`, so it needs no implementation evidence. It has no implementation edges and the review roots are empty.

I checked each clause for a prescribed library, algorithm, signature, type, field or delegation:

- "A successful `ValidationContext::read` records the node's identity and the fingerprint of the returned contents" describes what `read` observes and records. `ValidationContext::read` is named only as the operation that has the behavior. The text does not prescribe its signature or the types it uses. Any implementation that records the same identity and fingerprint on success meets the clause, including one that stores the observations elsewhere.
- "A failed read records no successful observation" is an observable outcome.
- "The evidence becomes stale when a later read of that node has a different fingerprint" is observable behavior. The text delegates it to `requirements.sdk.graph.evidence.checking_records`, which is cited and supplies context only.
- "For a Rust caller, the SDK records the fingerprint when `read` returns the contents" and the agent "delivery" rule about the provider responding successfully are timing and semantic rules. They say which version's fingerprint is recorded, not how the code is organized. A different internal design could still record the fingerprint of the content the model actually saw.

The `{cite}` references to `requirements.sdk.graph.evidence.node_inputs` and `requirements.sdk.graph.evidence.checking_records` give context only. They need no coverage.

behavioral: The reviewed tests cover each obligation in `requirements.sdk.graph.validation-context.read_node.inputs`.

**Rust caller, successful read.** `crates/trust-but-verify/src/graph/validation_tests.rs#fn[snapshots_record_exact_reads_and_retain_distinct_versions]` checks that `read` and `read_snapshot` record `Dependency::Node(identity, fp(contents))`. It also checks that the record gets `fp("before")` and then `fp("after")` after the contents change.

`#fn[direct_reads_return_complete_unicode_contents_and_snapshots]` runs the same check on empty contents and on large multi-byte Unicode contents. The recorded fingerprint equals the full original contents.

**Failed read records nothing.** The direct-read failure on node 9 in `#fn[direct_reads_return_complete_unicode_contents_and_snapshots]` returns the error `"missing"` and leaves `dependencies()` empty. The read of node 2 in `#fn[snapshots_record_exact_reads_and_retain_distinct_versions]` errors and adds no dependency.

In `crates/trust-but-verify/src/agent/tests.rs#fn[node_preparation_tool_errors_allow_recovery_without_recording_undelivered_contents]`, the agent's `read_node` fails with `unsupported node contents`. The tool error is delivered and `dependencies()` is empty.

**Staleness.** In `#fn[snapshots_record_exact_reads_and_retain_distinct_versions]` and `#fn[direct_reads_return_complete_unicode_contents_and_snapshots]`, the record has fingerprints taken before a content change. `record.is_current(...)` is asserted false afterwards. The failure to resolve is covered by `requirements.sdk.graph.evidence.checking_records`, which this requirement only cites, so it needs no test here.

**Agent delivery.** In `#fn[graph_tools_record_delivered_snapshots_and_prepared_pages_do_not_record_delivery]`, a `read_node` call that is followed by a provider failure records no dependency. A successful run records `Dependency::Node(2, 18000-char fingerprint)`, and the usage counters distinguish prepared inputs from delivered ones.

**The `3` versus `4` example.** `#fn[graph_read_pages_retain_the_prepared_snapshot_after_contents_change]` has a `ChangingProvider` that replaces the contents while the provider is handling the request that carries the `read_node` result. The recorded fingerprint equals the original contents. The graph is read exactly once (`reads == [1]`), so the node is not re-read. The later pages also reproduce the original contents.

All of these tests carry `{test}` markers for the subject.

:::{req} node_inputs
Finishing a verification includes every successful tracked node read in its
`Fingerprinted`, whether ordinary code or a model tool requested it. Each observation
contains the node identity and the fingerprint of the contents actually supplied.
A failed read returns an error without inventing a successful observation.
Repeating an identical observation adds no information. Reading the same
identity with two different fingerprints preserves both observations.
:::{req} checking_records
The method is declared under {cite}`requirements.sdk.graph.running-criteria.check_inputs`.
The method resolves the recorded dependencies through graph operations and
fingerprinting, comparing each with its saved observation. A fingerprint
mismatch returns `Ok(false)` and permits an early return; it need not resolve
later dependencies. An encountered dependency-resolution failure returns an
error.
The method observes the current state that the caller intends to inspect.
Freshness checking has a separate observation scope from criterion execution.
Checked observations enter the new trace when execution explicitly reads
or delivers them.
A checked snapshot can be reused if it still represents the current state.
